To become as strong at Go as you can: to keep improving, game after game, toward grandmaster-level play. The concrete target is to win consistently against the strongest opponent on the ladder, the 9d profile.

## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.

I’ll read the last two reviews, retain the 20k opponent, and focus on building viable bases and recounting area as boundaries change. I’ll play to completion and save the game and lessons for the next session.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi 7, simple ko.
White54/Black55 passes ended the game; board() confirmed B+18.
Independent area Black53/White28+7, neutral0/dead0, matches the result.
Physical captures: Black9/White2. White36 J1 captured H2/J2; Black51 J2 captured all nine right stones.

Read97/96 and consulted30. Confirmed empty White board, then selected20k before Black1G7.
game-098.sgf records all55 actual moves, including the final passes.
game-098-log.json preserves initial board, selection, all27 play responses and final confirmation:30 full raw snapshots, plus live notes and replay verification.
game-098-verification.js inspects supplied boards and replays actual recorded history only.
All55 moves replayed legally; all30 snapshots matched boards, physical captures, next-move numbers and ko markers.
Black28 turns minus one pass minus two captured=25 final stones.
White27 turns minus one pass minus nine captured=17.
No refused move, ko, resignation, transport error or play-response loss occurred.

Code counted current groups/liberties/regions and explicit targets, kept records, converted actual history to SGF and replayed actual moves.
Every move and hypothetical continuation was chosen/read manually.
No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, automated move selection/ranking/recommendation or delegated agent was used.
The selected36 count at15 and group inspections35/49 were live. The corrected37 complete outline, exact final ledger and full replay were retrospective.
No optimal opening, winning replacement, exhaustive earlier rescue or individual move value was established. Game52's scoring discrepancy remains separate.

## Exact moves

${g.moves.map(m=>m.number+" "+m.color+" "+m.move).join(", ")}.

C3 began opposite BlackG7. BlackD3/C2 pressed immediately.
C5 broadened upward, then C4 at6 joined C3/C5 after C3 was reduced to B3/C4.
BlackB3 removed the remaining lower liberty but the joined chain retained five liberties.
C7 at8 added an open upper-left base. C7 initially remained separate.

The live selected outline at15 was:
A/B/C rows4–9=18;
D/E rows7–9=6;
F/G/H/J rows1–3=12;
total36, with no Black occupation included.
Three White physical groups had no completed eyes.
This selected outline OMITTED the already-existing WhiteC3 stone.
The retrospective complete outline therefore adds C3 for37.
It was still below White38 required to win when all81 points are assigned.
Do not call C3 a genuine later territorial gain simply because the selected target omitted it.

D5/E5/E6/E7/E8 at16–24 formed a joined center boundary.
BlackE4/F5/F6/F8 pressed beside it.
E9 at38 retained the top endpoint before BlackF9.
C6 at40 actually joined isolatedC7 to the main.
D7 at42 joined C7/E7 and completed trueD6, bounded by C6/D5/E6/D7 in the same main.
B5/A5 at44/46 retained the fifth-row edge after BlackB4, but A4/B4 were lost.
D4 at48 joined C4/D5 and claimed the mixed boundary point.
C8/C9 at50/52 enclosed D8/D9 independently of D6.
The left development was viable, but its final28 could not offset the right loss.

## Right base: connection and a planned divider were insufficient

G3 at10 took the open lower-right corner after BlackF4.
BlackG4/H4 capped the top while H3/F3 at12/14 joined and expanded the lower boundary.
BlackE3 pressed from the left.
This gave a prospective twelve-point F/G/H/J rows1–3 base, not secure life.

BlackF2/F1 at25/27 undercut F1/F2.
G2 at26 joined G3 and retained the G-column lower boundary.
J4 at28 reserved the upper edge; BlackJ5 left it soleJ3.
J3 at30 correctly saved and joined J4 to H3/main.
That was an actual connection, but J3 was now a STONE and could not simultaneously serve as a vacant upper eye.
The remaining lower room was G1/H1/H2/J1/J2; G1 touched BlackF1 and was not a true White eye.

H1 at32 began isolated with G1/H2/J1 liberties.
The intended next J2 would have divided shared trueH2/J1 eyes between H1 and the main.
The plan required another move before the opponent invaded.
Black33 J2 entered immediately, with H2/J1 liberties, defeating that divider.
The failure was a concrete unprotected two-move life plan after the undercut.
No earlier alternative has been proved winning or an exhaustive earlier rescue established.

G1 at34 joined H1 to G2/main.
Now all eight right stones and BlackJ2 shared ONLY H2/J1.
This was not established seki or life.
Black35 H2 joined J2; both the White eight and Black pair had soleJ1.
White36 J1 legally captured H2/J2 and saved the eight stones.
After rebuilding, the nine White stones had only H2/J2: one CONNECTED two-point room.
The capture opened one eye space, not two.

Black37 E2 joined F2/F1 to the central main; it did not rescue White.
Black49 H2 re-entered the two-point room.
Live inspection showed White nine soleJ2 and BlackH2 soleJ2.
The tempting UNPLAYED WhiteJ2 would capture H2, but all TEN White stones would then have soleH2.
BlackH2 would legally recapture ten, without simple ko.
This limited line was read manually and not played; it explains why the immediate capture was futile.
It is not a proof of every earlier position's forced outcome.

White50 C8 secured the surviving left instead.
Black51 J2 captured the nine actual right stones:
F3/G1/G2/G3/H1/H3/J1/J3/J4.
Black53 G2 joined the H2/J2 capturers to the main through F2.
No speculative late entry was played after failing to establish a useful second-eye route.

## Final area and exact ledger

White17 stones plus11 territory=28.
All17 form one physical group.
TrueD6 has four White boundaries C6/D5/E6/D7.
D8/D9 is a separate two-point eye space bounded by C8/C9/D7/E8/E9.
A6/A7/A8/A9/B6/B7/B8/B9 is another eight-point room.
Life does not depend on treating that large room as eight individual eyes.

Black25 stones plus28 territory=53:
upper-right G8/G9/H7/H8/H9/J6/J7/J8/J9 nine;
G5/G6/H5 three;
captured-right F3/G3/H3/J3/J4 five;
lower-left A1/A2/A3/B1/C1/D1/D2/E1 eight;
G1/H1/J1 three.
Black has four physical groups; official scoring retained all stones.
This count agrees with the result without an exhaustive independent life proof for every Black group.
No dead-stone adjustment or neutral area was needed.

Complete corrected early37:
left25 minusA4/B4 two plusD4/D5/D6/E5/E6 five=28;
right12 lost entirely;
total37−14+5=28.
E7/E8/E9 and D7/D8/D9 retained targets; they were not outside gains.
The original selected36 ledger is36−14+6=28, but its sixth “gain” C3 was already a White stone at15.
Use the corrected37 ledger when discussing genuine expansion.
FailedJ4 was outside the initial outline and gained nothing; do not subtract it again.
The nine physically captured stones were already included in the right-area loss, not nine extra area losses.
White's capture of H2/J2 temporarily restored included targets; it created no lasting outside gain.

53−(28+7)=18 matches B+18.
White54 passed after concrete left life and no viable outside route was established; Black55 passed.
All55 moves/30 snapshots are verified.

## Carry forward

Retain20k and read98/97; consult30 for broad viable development.
A planned divider that needs two moves must be checked against an immediate opponent entry.
After F2/F1 and J5, connecting J4 with J3 did not create an upper eye.
H1 required J2 next, but BlackJ2 occupied it first.
Before treating a base as viable, explicitly name the intended vacant eyes and check the opponent can occupy neither necessary divider nor eye point first.
No specific winning replacement has been proved.

Capturing two invaders can still leave exactly one two-point eye room.
After J1 captured H2/J2, the right group had only that connected room.
After BlackH2, WhiteJ2 would allow a legal ten-stone recapture atH2: no ko and no second eye.
The futile recapture was recognized and avoided, but the earlier life plan remained defective.

Include all existing friendly stones in a complete conditional outline, or label exclusions explicitly.
Live selected36 omitted C3; retrospective complete37 was still below38.
Actual left expansion netted three points, while the whole twelve-point right target died.
All17 surviving White joined one left main with trueD6 and independentD8/D9.
A successful left life proof does not repair an overall territorial deficit.
`;
store("review98",review);
text(await tools.apply_patch("*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: game-098.md\n+"+review.trimEnd().split("\n").join("\n+")+"\n*** End Patch"));

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
